title: Washington Heights
full_review:
An aspiring young comic illustrator must weigh ambition against responsibility when his father is shot and paralyzed during an attempted robbery in the modest drama "Washington Heights" (MAC). First-time director Alfredo de Villa's entry into "ethnic" filmmaking is undermined by the protagonist's all-too-familiar dilemma: how to escape his dead-end neighborhood while maintaining his cultural identity.

Carlos Ramirez (Manny Perez) hails from Washington Heights in New York City, where his father, Eddie (Tomas Milian), runs a local bodega. The artistically gifted Carlos dreams of penning his own comic books and moving downtown with his girlfriend, Maggie (Andrea Navedo) -- a career path frowned upon by the more pragmatic Eddie, whose immigrant work ethic kept him from pursuing his own dream of becoming a mambo singer. Likewise, his best friend Mickey Kilpatrick's (Danny Hoch) loopy visions of becoming a world-class bowler are met with derision by his own father, Sean (Jude Ciccolella), the no-nonsense, meat-and-potato superintendent of Eddie and Carlos' apartment building.

Carlos' dreams are tragically put on hold when a strung-out junkie pops a bullet in Eddie's spine, leaving him paralyzed from the waist down. Eddie's dire medical condition necessitates that Carlos not only care for his father but also that he take the helm in running the bodega -- a situation muddied by a foggy subplot concerning monies owed by Eddie to Sean.

With little choice, Carlos complies -- working at the bodega by day while burning the midnight oil with his drawings. Resentment quickly boils over. The new arrangement also provides the perfect arena for Carlos to confront Eddie about past marital infidelities and the emotional toll they exacted from Carlos' mother -- a pain she took with her to the grave.

Carlos' situation turns from bad to worse when Mickey's harebrained scheme to punch their tickets out of the barrio -- involving stealing money from Maggie's volatile brother, Angel (Bobby Cannavale) -- results in deadly consequences.

The film succeeds in capturing the Latin flavor of Washington Heights without reverting to ethnic stereotypes. And while Carlos and Mickey's salsa-and-corned-beef-friendship effectively reflects the heterogeneity of the culturally diverse neighborhood, the motivation propelling them through the narrative -- a burning desire to escape their dead-end existence -- is one viewers have seen countless times in a slew of other independent films -- a weakness compounded by the trite transgenerational angst-driven subplot.

One troubling aspect of the film is Eddie's ambiguous moral misgivings about his womanizing. During one scene Eddie laments his philandering, expressing regret over his past infidelities. Yet later on, when Carlos, wrestling with guilt over cheating on Maggie, asks his father for advice, Eddie offers a glib response, quickly followed by a cavalier remark about his own proclivity for the senoritas. The exchange plays like a verbal winking nod of approval, inconsistent with Eddie's earlier mea culpa.

Due to sexual situations with nudity, violence and recurring rough language and vulgarities, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
